title: Market's Nvidia obsession obscuring an opportunity in this name
summary: Investors might be overlooking Disney earnings.
body: The market is unable to divert its attention from anything not related to the ongoing saga that is Nvidia and its embattled former CEO Jensen Huang. It's understandable, given both the detail of the story and Nvidia impact on the market. It remains the tech story du jour, and it's getting plenty of ink. I think investors should remember there are other big names reporting this week outside of Nvidia that deserve time and attention. One such name is The Walt Disney Company (DIS) . After a prolonged period of strategic transitions, the company may finally be turning the corner. Driven by a renewed focus on the bottom line, management's cost discipline now supports a runway for double-digit earnings-per-share (EPS) gains through fiscal 2027, even as it continues to trade at about its 5-year average forward multiple of 14.3x, well below the broad market multiple of more than 18x. Trading back to a market multiple, justified if it establishes above-market EPS growth, suggests ~26% upside, which is also consistent with a sum-of-the-parts analysis that points to an intrinsic valuation of $140 to $160 per share versus the Friday, November 13th closing price of $118.97. Despite broader macroeconomic anxieties, the theme park and cruise divisions are showing surprisingly resilient demand. Domestically, the metrics are highly encouraging: attendance is climbing, and more importantly, per-capita spending continues to rise. On the digital front, Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) Disney's streaming margins currently sit in the low teens, respectable given the segment's previous lack of profits. But the real upside scenario requires looking ahead: if Disney can scale these DTC margins to 20% or higher, the stock could at least trade at a multiple comparable to streaming king Netflix (which would imply a share price of ~ $139 or so. With linear TV stabilizing, the parks firing on all cylinders, and streaming marching toward higher profitability, Disney offers a highly asymmetric risk-reward profile. The magic is returning to Disney's financials, and the current share price heavily discounts a business fundamentally engineered for double-digit growth. Right now, the options market is pricing a ~6% move by the end of the week (the company reports Tuesday, pre-open), which is below the 8 quarter median move of 7.4%. Anticipating a "vol crush" after earnings, I like selling December premium to help finance the purchase of a longer-dated call - a diagonal call/spread risk reversal. When selecting an option trade consider the key things that affect its value and how those things differ from simply buying (or selling) the underlying asset. For these option trades, let's consider three sensitivities (Greeks): Delta, the rate at which the option position changes in value for changes in the underlying price. Theta, or decay, which measures how much the value of an option declines as time passes, and Vega, the change in an option's price associated with changes in the implied volatility of an option. In the case of the diagonal risk reversal each of these factors plays into the structure to our benefit. The delta of the structure is less than 100, meaning that the p&l associated with moves up or down will be less for one spread than they would be for 100 shares of stock. We like this because the stock has already had a decent run recently, and the option structure will lose less than the stock will if it gives that back. Because nearer dated expiration decay more rapidly as a percentage of the options value than longer dated options do (and out of the money options also exhibit accelerated decay), the shorter dated December options we're selling should decay in value more quickly than the longer dated March options we are buying, even though the March option has a higher premium. body: For chip stocks, the rule adds a regulatory hit to a sector already weighed down by the Nvidia leadership turmoil. AMD and CoreWeave fell 5% or more and Nvidia about 4%. Licensing requirements in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore cloud the outlook for the region’s fast-growing data center trade, a source of demand for US chips. The TSMC provision brings Taiwan’s chip supply chain into scope, which could weigh on Asian tech names. The bigger near-term risk is Beijing’s response during Trump’s China trip this week. Retaliation or stalled trade talks would add to the pressure. Washington is closing the side door that let Chinese firms rent American AI chips through Southeast Asian data centers. The bigger surprise is that the Commerce Department’s own rule had to be written by other agencies. The US Commerce Department has issued a rule requiring licenses for shipments of advanced chips from Nvidia and other US companies to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported. The aim is to stop Chinese customers from tapping AI computing power remotely through data centers in those countries. The rule takes effect immediately, with a 60-day window for company comments, and US tech firms may be able to obtain exceptions. It would also make it harder for data center operators anywhere in the world to give Chinese companies remote access to AI chips. And it would make it harder for Chinese chip designers to work with TSMC, the world’s leading contract chipmaker. The rule targets the network of companies that have used Nvidia chips to build data centers across Southeast Asia and rent that capacity to Chinese technology groups trying to catch up in AI. The Journal singled out Megaspeed International, a firm linked to the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive last week. How the rule was produced is as notable as what it says. The Bureau of Industry and Security normally drafts chip-export measures. Its release said this rule had been written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council. Export-control specialists called that highly unusual. One former State Department official said it suggested Commerce had resisted the rule until the White House forced it to act. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has accused Commerce of holding up action on Megaspeed and export-control loopholes for months, adding to pressure on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Officials have said the department was wary of upsetting Beijing during trade talks. President Donald Trump defended Lutnick on Monday. He said the delay made sense to avoid a blowup at a time when relations with China are good. Shares of AI and data center companies, including Advanced Micro Devices and CoreWeave, fell 5% or more after the announcement, and Nvidia closed around 4% lower. The timing is awkward, coming just as Trump travels to China this week with both Lutnick and Bessent. Lawmakers are also pushing for tougher chip-export rules in this year’s defense spending package. But these signs of normalization have yet to reach the airline industry, where jet fuel prices remain eye-wateringly high and hedging contracts are expiring. It seems not all airlines will survive the winter. Airlines have been among the sectors to feel the most immediate pain from the fallout of the war between the United States and Israel, and Iran. With jet fuel representing a solid portion of the industry’s expenses, the fuel price jump following the squeeze on Hormuz tanker traffic immediately hit airlines. The problem now is that the war has gone on longer than pretty much anyone expected. Airlines’ fuel price hedge contracts are expiring, and they are in a delicate position. Jet fuel is currently trading at a little below $150 per barrel. This is off peaks of some $180 per barrel hit last month, but it is still substantially higher than the $85 per barrel airlines paid for their fuel before the war began. The outlook, according to industry executives, is not really optimistic. “Our view is that we are facing a new normal where the fuel price is there to stay at the levels that we see more or less today,” Air Astana’s chief executive Ibrahim Canliel told Reuters in an interview last week. The executive was referring to the prospect of oil prices remaining between $90 and $100 per barrel. Indeed, even with all the talk about a glut returning, Brent crude remains above $95 per barrel, and the chances of it falling below $90 would likely need more than a series of reports suggesting a return to oversupply. “I think it's most likely that fuel stays high,” the chief executive of United Airlines, Scott Kirby, said at the Yahoo Finance Invest event, as quoted by Yahoo Finance. “It is increasing the stress. I think six of 10 US airlines are going to lose money this year. And a lot of people are sort of managing with … the strategy that we hope fuel prices will go down. I think it's going to lead to a reckoning.” Hoping that prices would go down is not really a strategy, when you get right down to it. Unfortunately, there aren’t many alternatives to that, and now many airlines need to make a difficult decision. Hedging contracts inked earlier this year are now expiring. Airlines could either negotiate new ones, which would feature the current jet fuel prices, or not hedge, potentially facing even higher jet fuel prices but also the possibility of a price slump that would be very welcome. It is a genuine dilemma and, for some, likely the difference between survival and bankruptcy. In Europe alone, airlines are “bleeding cash”, as The Telegraph put it , with an extra $12 billion added to their collective jet fuel bill so far as a result of the war-related supply disruption. Now, they are also facing their low season as air travel declines over the winter, with a bonus demand killer in the face of higher ticket prices driven by the jet fuel supply squeeze. “This is a very challenging time and it’s going to get even tougher as hedges roll off towards the end of the financial year in March,” a former British Airways network planner told The Telegraph. “We can expect to see more airlines in trouble. Uganda’s dream to achieve its first commercial oil production and crude exports has been delayed yet again, extending the country’s wait to more than two decades since commercial oil reserves were first discovered in the country in 2006. Officials from the Uganda National Oil Company (UNOC) and the Petroleum Authority of Uganda (PAU) have announced that Uganda’s first oil production and exports have now been pushed back to before the end of June 2027, blaming the delay on international supply chain bottlenecks and disruptions linked to the war in Iran. According to the PAU , the Middle East conflict delayed key equipment and material deliveries such as parts for metering, electrical instrumentation and telecommunications systems required to finalize the production and evacuation infrastructure. The delay will create a rather substantial hole in the country’s budget, with Uganda’s Finance Minister Henry Musasizi telling parliament in June that the Ush 84.39 trillion budget for FY 2026/2027 had projected petroleum revenues of Ush 1.44 trillion (~$380 million). According to Ugandan officials, while construction work at the $5.6-billion East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) is more than 90% complete, critical supporting facilities such as pump stations three and four and the pipeline’s electrical, instrumentation, telecommunications and security systems are still incomplete, requiring coordinated testing and commissioning across the EACOP, Tilenga, Kingfisher and Tanga projects. Lawmakers put the Tilenga Project at 78% complete and the Kingfisher development at 90% in October; however, the Central Processing Facilities (CPFs) required to treat and stabilize the raw crude are still undergoing final installation and pre-commissioning. Additionally, the 1,443-kilometre EACOP heated export pipeline linking western Uganda to Tanga Port in Tanzania requires the system to be thermally integrated to operate safely before any oil can move due to the waxy nature of Ugandan crude. Uganda is projected to achieve a combined peak output of about 230,000 barrels of oil per day across TotalEnergies’ (NYSE:TTE) Tilenga project and CNOOC’s Kingfisher project. Production is expected to kick off with an initial rate of around 25,000 barrels per day from the Kingfisher field, rising to the field’s 40,000-barrel-per-day capacity, while Tilenga ramps up toward its 190,000-barrel-per-day peak. body: Diamondback to Buy Double Eagle’s Midland Stake for $5 Billion What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… The AI boom is pushing developers to test a new frontier for positioning data centers, following the growing backlash against the excessive use of land, water, and energy resources onshore. So hyperscalers and start-ups have moved to test placing data centers under the sea or floating on ships, to save on water, land, and electricity use. Data centers in the ocean could significantly reduce freshwater and power use for cooling and could source electricity from offshore wind farms or tidal wave power projects, reducing concerns among communities about the impact of onshore data centers on their water, environment, and energy sources. However, burying massive data centers under water creates new challenges and raises new environmental issues such as the impact on marine life and habitats, and new operational challenges, including how repairs on remote undersea data centers would work. No solution for picking a site for a data center is ideal, but a growing number of companies have proposed underwater data centers to bypass mounting community opposition to land AI centers and show off environmental positives such as powering proposed subsea centers with offshore wind. In one of the best-known pilots in the ocean, Microsoft’s Project Natick tested in the 2010s operations in a data center submerged to the seafloor offshore Scotland’s Orkney Islands. The structure, the size of a shipping container, proved the concept of underwater data centers is feasible, as well as logistically, environmentally, and economically practical, Microsoft said in 2020. But four years later, Noelle Walsh, President of Cloud Operations and Innovation at Microsoft, confirmed to Data Center Dynamics in 2024 that the underwater project was discontinued. The hyperscaler didn’t give a concrete reason for the halt, but said it would apply the learnings to other cases. Yet, Walsh told DCD, “I'm not building subsea data centers anywhere in the world.” Two years later, other companies are proposing subsea data centers, including offshore Maine and Alaska. Meanwhile, China this summer launched the world’s first offshore wind-powered underwater data center, using seawater cooling and renewable electricity to reduce energy, water, and land requirements. Chinese research showed this month that China holds 80% of the world’s patents for underwater data centers. In the U.S. and Europe, subsea data centers are likely to face much more backlash than in China because of the way they could change marine habitat and potentially endanger marine life. While seawater could act as a free sink with cold water to cool data centers, potential warming of the areas close to a submerged data center pod, capsule, or other structure could change habitats. At-scale commercial operations of underwater data centers are years away, but this year has seen several proposals from start-ups to install subsea or floating data centers offshore. Delaware-based DeepGreen Cook Inlet is proposing a 1,650-acre underwater hyperscale data center in Alaska. Environmentalists say the impacts of concern include noise interference with marine life, including the endangered beluga whales, electromagnetic frequency (EMF) exposure to marine life that directly affects salmon and beluga whales, warming water temperature, and copper pollution. The net was cast wide, as several major possibilities in the world’s main aggregate source of hydrocarbons had already moved more firmly in the run-up to the invasion into China’s and Russia’s sphere of influence. This included Saudi Arabia and the UAE, both of whose de facto leaders refused even to take a telephone call from then-President Joe Biden to talk about helping to reduce spiralling oil and gas prices by producing more, as analysed in full in my latest book on the new global oil market order . Qatar was a notable early exception in the region, becoming such a key supplier of liquefied natural gas to European allies of the U.S. that it was designated a ‘Major Non-NATO Ally’, as was Egypt, which had a multilayered strategic importance to the West, as it did to the East, as also detailed in the book . Perhaps the most unexpected country to which Washington and its allies directed their attention was Libya, but investment plans were made and money flowed in, helping to push its oil production up to a 13-year high of 1.4-1.5 million barrels per day (bpd). Archayev said in early October that TAPI’s continuation towards southern Afghanistan’s Kandahar Province would remain a Turkmen government priority in 2027. But he added that a funding level had yet to be finalized and no specific construction targets had been set. Pakistan’s and India’s interest in gaining access to Turkmen gas appeared to be waning in the early 2020s. "We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear. The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses , but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed. With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI. Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend. It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island. Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said. Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear. The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his longstanding critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs. Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking. The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event. Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said. "To the extent our economy is a free-market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about." Warsh returned repeatedly to one scenario for the economy that draws on past experience. The so-called China shock unfolded after that country joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and moved heavily into low-cost manufacturing. According to Marketscreener , the retreat reflects a reversal of speculative investment demand, easing physical shortages and a less favourable interest-rate outlook. The most recent Silver Institute/Metals Focus figures that were released on Nov. 12 provide a useful picture of the market, showing demand falling, mine production down slightly year over year and recycling up six per cent. The market balance (supply over demand) is also dropping, now at a projected 35-million ounce deficit in 2026. That’s down from a 54-million ounce deficit in 2025 and 124-million ounce deficit in 2024. Of the just over one billion ounces of silver produced annually, 80 per cent of it comes from mining, with the balance generated through recycling. Mexico, China, Peru, Chile and Bolivia are the top five countries by supply, generating just over 500 million ounces each year. Approximately 70 to 80 per cent of global silver output is produced as a by-product of mining for other metals – primarily copper, lead and zinc. Lead-zinc mines produce 32 per cent of that by-product output, while 25 per cent comes from copper mines. This constrains supply, as silver production cannot respond quickly to higher prices. Only about 28 per cent of 2026 mine production is expected to come from primary silver mines. The rest depends heavily on production decisions made for other commodities, a relatively inelastic supply response. The top five uses for silver (as a percentage of total demand) are industrial (42 per cent), photovoltaics (18 per cent), jewellery (18 per cent), coins/bars (15 per cent) and silverware (5 per cent). Central banks have no significant silver holdings. Inflation and interest rates are critical: Higher real yields and a stronger U.S. dollar have been major obstacles to a price recovery. A sustained decline in U.S. 10-year real treasury yields would be one of the strongest signals of improving conditions for precious metals. If inflation rises and interest rates remain relatively stable, or, even better, if inflation is subdued and interest rates gradually decline – the best environment for the silver price – real interest rates fall. When real interest rates are below zero (i.e. a negative yield), the cost to hold silver (or gold), which does not pay any interest and therefore has no yield, is better than a negative real return on other assets. body: Tech firms dragged Asian stock markets down again Tuesday as the fallout from the Nvidia crisis continued to rattle trading floors, with US moves to tighten restrictions on Chinese access to chips adding to uncertainty. The selloff comes as investors brace for the release of earnings from the Wall Street titan, which comes days after boss Jensen Huang resigned over revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Also in focus is the initial public offering of Claude-creator Anthropic, which is being seen as a test of confidence in the AI trade, which has been whipsawed in recent months by concerns over companies' eye-watering AI investments and their profitability. Markets have been battered since the crisis broke at Nvidia, which is at the centre of a buildout in artificial intelligence that has helped propel global markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the world. The tech-heavy Nasdaq led steep losses Monday on Wall Street as traders continued to assess the latest developments. And Asia again followed suit, with Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei -- home to the region's biggest AI-linked firms -- again taking the brunt of the selling, with all three down at least one percent. There were also big losses in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore and Wellington. Nvidia's earnings will be closely watched after the market closes later Tuesday, with investors looking for signs of whether the AI boom can withstand the widening scandal. Matt Weller at Forex.com said: "Data centre demand and guidance will be central. "Investors will look for evidence that hyperscalers and other customers are sustaining their spending on AI infrastructure, and whether fourth-quarter guidance points to further growth." body: Analysts closely watch Nvidia as a bellwether for AI and the wider stock market. Nvidia surpassed Wall Street expectations for revenue over a recent three-month period, the company said on Wednesday, demonstrating strong performance as a data center boom drives demand for the company's advanced artificial intelligence chips. The California-based company recorded $96.2 billion in sales over three months ending in July, which beat a Bloomberg forecast of $92 billion. The jump in revenue marked 106% growth compared to the same quarter a year earlier. In recent years, Nvidia has defied skeptics with blockbuster revenue quarter after quarter, despite political backlash against data centers and looming concern about a financial bubble in AI. Rip-roaring growth transformed Nvidia from an ascendant AI player into the world's most valuable company. The results hold implications well beyond Nvidia. Many analysts view the company as a bellwether for the stock market and the overall economy, which have both come to rely in part on massive spending on AI. As big-tech names spend hundreds of billions on chips and data centers necessary for the energy-intensive technology, however, the financial benefits remain uncertain. The earnings reported by Nvidia offered a gauge of demand for a key building block of AI, showing whether appetite for the technology remains at a fever pitch. Before the earnings report, Karan Girotra, a professor of operations, technology, and innovation at Cornell Tech, said investors would watch whether the company has retained its dominance in chip manufacturing. As opposed to the highly competitive markets for AI models and enterprise products, the chip sector has given way to a clear winner. Nvidia "does not face a serious challenger at its layer of the stack and is probably the best chance for public market investors to profit from the AI boom," Girotra said. Fears of an AI bubble persisted ahead of Nvidia’s previous earnings report, but the company rebuked naysayers. Nvidia recorded $81.6 billion in sales over three months ending in April, which beat analyst expectations of $79.2 billion. The jump in revenue marked 85% growth compared to the same quarter a year earlier. Despite Nvidia's continued expansion, investors have proven jittery in recent months. Shares have climbed 13% so far this year after soaring nearly 39% in 2025. The company boasts a market cap of $5.1 trillion, making it roughly equivalent to the GDP of Japan or Germany. Nvidia expanded at a breakneck pace after an AI craze set off by the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in 2022, soaring nearly 700% over the ensuing two years.

body: Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, its first since Jensen Huang's departure as CEO, with investors watching for signs of whether the AI boom can withstand the widening scandal that toppled him. Its shares fell 4 percent on Monday, extending a slide of more than 12 percent since the scandal erupted, and the stock has lost more than 25 percent over the past month amid growing doubts about the health of the AI investment boom. The results will be the first presented under Nvidia's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO. "I can't imagine it would be business as usual," said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer, describing the company as in turmoil. "If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn't be well received," he added. Analysts will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang's aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies. That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy, with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Thursday. Luke Rahbari, CEO of Equity Armor Investments, which holds Nvidia shares, said Kress would likely face pointed questions about the company's financing commitments to AI firms. "Are you going to honor those? What are you going to do with those?" he said. He said investors would also closely watch Nvidia's guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore. Singapore is at the heart of the scandal that brought Huang down. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company with Chinese links, is under US criminal investigation for potentially helping to shift Nvidia's most powerful technology to China in violation of US rules. The scandal erupted on November 8 when The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang and Megaspeed executive Alice Huang -- who are not related -- were romantically linked, and that some within the US government suspected she might be a spy for China. The affair has exposed a rift within the Trump administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for an investigation into Jensen Huang's dealings with Megaspeed and accusing Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department of ignoring widespread reports that the company was shifting Nvidia technology to China. Facing criticism, the Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely, a step that also weighed on the company's shares. Tech tycoon Elon Musk and other major AI investors are meanwhile gathering signatures for an open letter calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement. "The most important time to help someone is when they're down," investor Bill Ackman said at a Semafor tech conference in California. Before leaving for summits in Asia, President Donald Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Huang back at Nvidia, waving off the security concerns. But given the legal cloud over him, most Wall Street analysts doubt that the AI rock star can return anytime soon to the company he founded 33 years ago. "No one individual can replace Jensen as CEO, but at the end of the day, after this global scandal, the old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good," said Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. Kress, a non-engineer, is not expected to stay in the role permanently, leaving Nvidia facing a high-stakes search for a successor.

body: Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) fell to their lowest level in more than four months as concerns over a slowdown in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry coincided with a stronger U.S. dollar. On Nov. 13, the three-month copper contract fell to an intraday low of $13,456 per ton, down approximately 10% from its record high in September. The price marked its lowest level since mid-July and extended its decline to a fifth consecutive week. The decline has been driven largely by weakness in AI-related technology stocks and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia’s leadership change. Investors are concerned that the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang could disrupt financing for AI data center projects, an area in which Nvidia has played a major role. Expectations that construction of data centers and expansion of power grids could be delayed are weighing on copper futures, given the metal’s importance to both sectors. UBS said Nvidia had served as a major source of financing for emerging cloud operators known as neoclouds and AI developers. The bank warned that new financing commitments and infrastructure investments could temporarily slow during the leadership transition. JPMorgan also said existing agreements were likely to remain in place, but negotiations for new data center financing could take longer and borrowing costs could rise. Goldman Sachs, however, attributed the recent decline in copper prices more to changes in investor positioning than to a deterioration in physical supply and demand. The bank said that even as data center construction continues, investors are pricing in the possibility of slower AI capital expenditure and reducing their long positions in copper futures. Democrats’ gains in the U.S. midterm elections and their projected control of both chambers in the next Congress have also heightened market caution. Expectations that increased congressional oversight could slow data center investment have weighed on the outlook for copper demand. John Meyer, an analyst at SP Angel, identified selling in AI-related stocks and the possibility of delays in data center construction as key factors behind the decline in copper prices. China’s sluggish economic recovery has added to the downward pressure. Growth in industrial production slowed in October, while weak consumer spending persisted in the world’s largest copper-consuming country, raising concerns about future demand. The upcoming earnings call is drawing particular attention as the first to be held under Kress following Huang’s resignation. Investors are seeking clarity not only on the outlook for AI business growth but also on whether Nvidia will change its financing and investment strategy toward data center customers and partners. In contrast to the selling pressure in financial markets, physical copper supply remains tight. body: Federal Reserve (Fed) Chair Kevin Warsh announced that the central bank has launched scenario analyses to assess the potential impact of artificial intelligence on the U.S. economy. According to remarks highlighted by Bloomberg TV on November 16, 2026, Fed researchers are examining several possible outcomes, including faster economic growth, rising unemployment, and investments in artificial intelligence failing to meet expectations. Warsh emphasized that the widespread adoption of AI could have significant implications for future monetary policy. He also stressed that the studies are intended to prepare for potential economic developments rather than serve as forecasts. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh discussed the role of artificial intelligence in economic transformation at the Productivity and Employment Task Force Conference hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. According to the official speech published by the Federal Reserve , central bank researchers have begun modeling how the technology could affect economic growth and employment in the coming years. In the first scenario outlined by Warsh, artificial intelligence boosts productivity, pushing economic growth above its long-term average. If the benefits of technological progress are broadly shared between workers and capital owners, the U.S. economy could remain close to full employment. The second scenario presents a more complicated economic outlook. Although artificial intelligence could increase production and accelerate economic growth, automation might also displace a significant number of workers. Under such circumstances, economic activity could continue expanding even as the unemployment rate rises. The third scenario considers the possibility that elevated expectations surrounding artificial intelligence may not be fulfilled. Massive investments in technological infrastructure could fail to generate the anticipated returns, potentially triggering declines in stock market valuations and an economic slowdown. According to Warsh, such developments could lead to a substantial increase in unemployment while preventing the economy from realizing the expected productivity gains. In the statement shared by Bloomberg TV on X , Warsh emphasized preparations to understand how the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence could affect the world's largest economy. The Fed Chair believes the technology could do more than transform existing business processes, potentially accelerating the development of entirely new ideas. Warsh noted that artificial intelligence could differ from previous transformative technologies, such as electricity and the internal combustion engine. While earlier technological breakthroughs reshaped production processes, AI also has the potential to accelerate the generation of new ideas. However, Warsh emphasized that human decision-making would remain essential. He argued that even if artificial intelligence systems develop capabilities that surpass human knowledge, this would not necessarily eliminate the importance of human judgment and responsibility. The Fed Chair also warned that the misuse of artificial intelligence by malicious actors could create security threats to critical infrastructure. He therefore emphasized the importance of preparing for potential adverse consequences alongside the economic opportunities presented by the technology. An economic calendar is a table of fixed release dates for economic data and central bank decisions. Each row usually contains five items: the date, the time, the country, the indicator and three values. These three values are the previous figure (the last release), the forecast (the consensus of the economists surveyed) and the actual figure, which appears at the stated minute. For the price, the actual figure almost never counts on its own; what counts is how far it deviates from the forecast. Professionals call this the surprise. If inflation lands exactly on expectations, it is already priced in, and often little happens. body: With Nvidia set to report earnings, market attention is shifting from this quarter’s figures to next-quarter guidance and messages from its new leadership. Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang (젠슨 황) has resigned, and CFO Colette Kress (콜레트 크레스) is serving as interim CEO. An assessment says next-quarter margin guidance and messaging on management continuity will be used as a basis for judgment by South Korea’s memory industry, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, as well as the stock market. Nvidia will announce its third-quarter results on Nov. 18. The release will be the first earnings announcement held without Huang as CEO. Huang stepped down after admitting an extramarital relationship with an executive at a customer, Megaspeed, and reports later emerged of suspected extramarital relationships with executives who reported directly to him. The board appointed Kress as interim CEO and is working with an external firm to find a permanent successor. With a leadership vacuum, what Kress says on the conference call has become a variable on the management side. Nvidia previously said on its August earnings call that supply bottlenecks would last until the end of fiscal 2028 and signalled full-scale mass production of its next-generation Vera Rubin platform. Whether the new leadership maintains that outlook and customer commitments is expected to affect management stability and the sustainability of customers’ businesses. An assessment says an Nvidia earnings beat is already treated as the baseline, and the stock has reacted to next-quarter figures. In four announcements from November last year to August this year, results all exceeded market forecasts, but the stock fell on the day three times. The stock fell in February despite an increase in data centre revenue, and again in May despite record-high revenue and free cash flow. The stock rose only in August, up 8.7 percent, when Nvidia presented next-quarter revenue along with next year’s growth outlook. As a result, next-quarter guidance, and gross margin in particular, has become the market’s biggest focus. Gross margin is the share of revenue left after subtracting costs, and it tends to shrink first when component prices rise. Nvidia cut its gross margin outlook for this quarter to 74 percent, plus or minus 0.5 percentage points, on its August earnings call, citing a shortage in memory supply, and said it expected the figure to fall to 71 to 72 percent by the end of this year. It has become important whether Nvidia held around 74 percent this quarter and whether next-quarter guidance stays near 74 percent. If it maintains the 74 percent level, that would be a more positive outcome than Nvidia’s projected decline path. The gross margin guidance also intersects with South Korea’s memory industry. Since Nvidia cited a memory supply shortage as the reason for lowering margins, a drop in next-quarter gross margin to 71 to 72 percent could be read as Nvidia absorbing rising memory prices. That would be a signal that memory suppliers’ pricing power is continuing. If Nvidia holds the 74 percent level, it could mean it has passed cost burdens on through selling prices or that memory procurement conditions have improved. If the supply bottleneck outlook is maintained, it can be interpreted as meaning that memory demand continues to outstrip supply. In addition, data centre revenue from China was under 1 percent in August, and questions have been raised over suspected chip exports, making Nvidia’s explanation of China sales another point to check. Nvidia recently warned in its proxy statement that a failure to establish an effective succession plan could hurt long-term performance, and CNN also pointed out that Nvidia lacked a talent pool and succession plan to replace Huang.
